summary:
Same-sex conduct between adults was decriminalised by the High Court in Jones v Attorney General in 2018, a ruling upheld on appeal. The challenge was brought by the activist Jason Jones, who stated publicly that he faced up to 25 years' imprisonment for consensual sex with an adult male partner, the maximum exposure under the criminal provisions at the time. Decriminalisation removed the threat of prosecution without producing legal gender recognition. The Trinidad and Tobago Transgender Coalition's director, Rae Alibey, said in 2024 that the trans community is the most marginalised group in the country and is not recognised in law: gender identity has no separate legal standing from sexual orientation, and institutional forms carry no gender-identity markers.

Entry rules still carry the older prohibition. Section 8 of the Immigration Act bars homosexual men and women who are not citizens from entering Trinidad and Tobago, and the provision is not known to have been enforced. In 2016 the Caribbean Court of Justice ruled that neither Trinidad and Tobago nor Belize had breached the freedom of movement of the Jamaican activist Maurice Tomlinson, but held that neither state may exclude gay nationals of CARICOM countries, because the Treaty of Chaguaramas obligations override the entry bans in domestic law.

Violence against LGBT+ people is reported through dating applications. Police warned in November 2024 that criminals create fake profiles to lure users to meetings that end in armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault, with two incidents reported in a single week. A newspaper editorial in June 2024 counted close to half a dozen app-related attacks over the preceding months. Superintendent Claire Guy-Alleyne said the legislation contains no specific hate-crime category.

No anti-discrimination protection was added by the 2024 constitutional review. The PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected the inclusion of sexual-orientation protections in the constitution, a decision announced at a special convention.

Custody carries known risk. The Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers, launched in November 2018 by the Caribbean Court of Justice, Caribbean judicial associations, UN Women and the JURIST Project, states that there are no special facilities in the penal system to accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities safely. It directs a judicial officer sentencing a person whose gender identity does not accord with their birth certificate to recommend to prison authorities that provisions be made for that inmate's physical safety, and instructs courts to address intersex and transgender people by their chosen pronoun and to admit them irrespective of dress. Housing for a trans prisoner therefore rests on a sentencing recommendation, and no dedicated facility exists.
tangentialFactors:
Partner recognition is absent. Trinidad and Tobago does not recognise same-sex marriage or civil unions, households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for the same rights and benefits as opposite-sex households, and same-sex couples cannot legally adopt. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex status has no mechanism for recognition, and the property consequences of separation are unsettled: in July 2018 Justice Frank Seepersad approved a property division between two male partners, noting their unequal treatment under current law and warning that without agreement the court would have had to rely on innovative applications of trust law.

Official rhetoric has run ahead of the statute in only one direction. In June 2016 Prime Minister Keith Rowley told Parliament that the state must protect all citizens "regardless of whom they sleep with", while refusing to repeal the criminal laws then in force. Two years later decriminalisation came from the High Court rather than from the executive or the legislature.
localsOnly: The 2009 University of the West Indies study commissioned by the Ministry of Social Development found that four of every five Trinbagonians believed in denying someone rights or equality on the basis of sexual orientation. That finding prompted the founding of CAISO, which works for public discussion and legislative protection. After the 2024 constitutional review, CAISO's Dr Angelique Nixon said the community has been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection. The Silver Lining Foundation works to end bullying of LGBTQ youth.
outOfScopeNotes:
Section 8 of the Immigration Act is not known to have been enforced, so how immigration officers treat a trans or visibly gender-nonconforming arrival at a port of entry is not sourced. Whether prison authorities act on the sentencing recommendations in the Gender Equality Protocol is likewise undocumented in the sources reviewed.

No national attitudinal research on gender identity has been carried out; the 2009 study covered sexual orientation. No figures were located on how many app-related attacks are reported by LGBT+ people, on prosecution or conviction practice since decriminalisation, or on the number of transgender people in the penal system. A 2012 travel and culture profile describes the criminal law as it stood before 2018 and does not reflect the current position.
